Hello, friend. Maybe I should give you a name, but that's a slippery slope. So let's skip the introductions and talk about why this blog exists: most people secure the wrong things. They buy a VPN and reuse one password across forty sites. They tape over the webcam and never install updates. Security isn't a product you buy. It's a set of decisions about what you're protecting, from whom, and how much effort it's worth. That's called a threat model, and you can build a useful one in fifteen minutes.

Why this blog exists

I write about security, Linux and the systems everyone depends on but nobody looks at. Not the movie version. The boring version: patches, logs, backups, clocks, the stuff that actually decides whether a bad day becomes a disaster. Everything here is defensive. If you came for exploits, there's nothing for you. If you came to understand your own machines better, stay.

A threat model in 15 minutes

Grab a text file. Answer four questions honestly.

  1. What do I have? Email (the master key to every password reset), your password manager, phone, laptop, cloud storage, bank, work accounts, photos you'd hate to lose.
  2. Who wants it? Realistically: automated credential-stuffing bots, opportunistic scammers, a thief who grabs your laptop at a café. Maybe an ex or a nosy coworker. Probably not a nation-state.
  3. How likely is each scenario? Reused passwords leaking in a breach: very likely. Phishing email: certain. Targeted hardware implant: no.
  4. What happens if it goes wrong? Losing email is catastrophic. Losing a forum account is an inconvenience. Spend your effort where likelihood and impact are both high.

That's it. You now know more about your risk than most organizations with a compliance binder.

The boring fixes that stop most attacks

For a typical person, three habits cover the overwhelming majority of real-world compromises.

Use a password manager

Every account gets a unique, random password. When a site gets breached, and it will, the damage stops at that site. Pick a reputable manager, protect it with a long passphrase, and let it generate everything else.

Turn on 2FA, prefer passkeys

Start with email, then your password manager, bank and code hosting. Passkeys and hardware security keys are phishing-resistant because the credential is bound to the real domain; a fake login page simply can't use it. Authenticator apps (TOTP) are a solid second choice. SMS is better than nothing, but SIM swaps are real.

Install updates

Most attacks use known, already-patched vulnerabilities. Turn on automatic updates for your OS, browser and phone. On Debian or Ubuntu, unattended upgrades take two commands:

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades

# check what's pending right now
apt list --upgradable
⚠️
Store your 2FA recovery codes somewhere offline. Locking yourself out is also a security failure.

What comes next

Revisit the threat model once a year, or whenever your life changes: a new job, a move, a public profile. The answers shift, and so should your defenses. The rest of this blog goes deeper, one system at a time: bits and bytes, debugging, daemons, vulnerabilities, backups, incidents, metadata, kernels. Read in any order.

And remember: the goal isn't to be unhackable. Nobody is. The goal is to be expensive enough that the attacker moves on to someone who didn't read this.

Everything on your machine is ones and zeroes. Your photos, your passwords, this sentence. Abstractions are comfortable, so most developers never look underneath. Then a file refuses to parse, a checksum doesn't match, or a network packet arrives "corrupted", and the only way to know what's really there is to read the bytes. This post is about learning to read them.

Bits, bytes and hex

A bit is 0 or 1. A byte is eight bits, so it holds 256 values: 0 to 255. Writing bytes in binary is noisy (11011110), and decimal hides the bit boundaries, so we use hexadecimal. One hex digit is exactly four bits, which means one byte is always exactly two hex digits.

DecimalBinaryHex
100000 10100x0A
1270111 11110x7F
2221101 11100xDE
2551111 11110xFF

Your shell can convert for you:

printf '%x\n' 222        # de
printf '%d\n' 0xde       # 222
echo 'obase=2; 222' | bc # 11011110

Bitwise operations

Bitwise operators work on each bit independently. They show up everywhere: file permissions, feature flags, network masks, hashing.

  • AND (&) keeps bits set in both. Use it to test or mask: flags & 0x04.
  • OR (|) sets bits: flags | 0x04.
  • XOR (^) flips bits where the operands differ. XOR-ing twice with the same value gets you back where you started.
  • Shifts (<<, >>) move bits left or right; 1 << 3 is 8.

Unix permissions are a clean example. chmod 640 is octal, three bits per digit: read (4), write (2), execute (1). So 6 is 110 (rw-), 4 is 100 (r--), 0 is nothing. An IPv4 netmask works the same way: 192.168.1.77 & 255.255.255.0 gives you the network, 192.168.1.0.

Endianness

When a number needs more than one byte, someone has to decide which byte goes first. Big-endian stores the most significant byte first; little-endian stores the least significant first. The 32-bit value 0x12345678 looks like this in memory:

big-endian:    12 34 56 78
little-endian: 78 56 34 12

x86 and most ARM systems are little-endian. Network protocols use big-endian, which is why it's called "network byte order" and why C has htons() and ntohl(). If an integer you parsed is absurdly large, check the byte order before you check anything else.

xxd and hexdump belong in your toolkit

File extensions lie. Bytes don't. Most formats start with a "magic number" that identifies them: PNG files begin with 89 50 4E 47, ELF binaries with 7F 45 4C 46, ZIP archives with 50 4B.

# first 32 bytes of a file, hex + ASCII
xxd -l 32 suspicious.pdf

# canonical hex+ASCII view
hexdump -C config.bin | head

# reverse a hex dump back into binary
xxd -p data.bin > data.hex

Everything on your machine is ones and zeroes. Your photos, your passwords, this sentence. Abstractions are comfortable, so most developers never look underneath. This post is about learning to read them.


Bits, bytes and hex

A bit is 0 or 1. A byte is eight bits, so it holds 256 values: 0 to 255. Writing bytes in binary is noisy (11011110), and decimal hides the bit boundaries, so we use hexadecimal. One hex digit is exactly four bits, which means one byte is always exactly two hex digits.

2221101 11100xDE
2551111 11110xFF





Your shell can convert for you:

printf '%x\n' 222        # de
printf '%d\n' 0xde       # 222
echo 'obase=2; 222' | bc # 11011110


Bitwise operations

Bitwise operators work on each bit independently. They show up everywhere: file permissions, feature flags, network masks, hashing.

 * AND (&) keeps bits set in both. Use it to test or mask: flags & 0x04.
 * OR (|) sets bits: flags | 0x04.
 * XOR (^) flips bits where the operands differ. XOR-ing twice with the same value gets you back where you started.
 * Shifts (<<, >>) move bits left or right; 1 << 3 is 8.

Unix permissions are a clean example. chmod 640 is octal, three bits per digit: read (4), write (2), execute (1). So 6 is 110 (rw-), 4 is 100 (r--), 0 is nothing. An IPv4 netmask works the same way: 192.168.1.77 & 255.255.255.0 gives you the network, 192.168.1.0.


Endianness

When a number needs more than one byte, someone has to decide which byte goes first. Big-endian stores the most significant byte first; little-endian stores the least significant first. The 32-bit value 0x12345678 looks like this in memory:

big-endian:    12 34 56 78

People think debugging is about fixing a mistake. It isn't. Debugging is about finding the root of the problem, and the fix is just what you do afterwards. In production, under pressure, with users waiting, the temptation is to change things until the error stops. That's how you end up with a fix you don't understand for a bug you never found. This is the method I use instead.

Reproduce first, theorize second

A bug you can't reproduce is a rumor. Before touching code, pin down the exact conditions: which input, which user, which version, which host, what time. Narrow the blast radius.

  • Does it happen for everyone or for one account?
  • Did it start with a deploy, a config change, or a traffic spike?
  • Does it happen on one node behind the load balancer but not the others?
  • Can you trigger it locally with production-like data?

Write the reproduction down as a test case the moment you have it. It becomes your regression test later.

Read the logs like evidence

Logs are a crime scene. Don't skim them for the first red line; build a timeline. Find the first anomaly, not the loudest one. The loud error at 03:14 is often a symptom of something quiet at 03:09.

# everything from one service since the deploy
journalctl -u api.service --since "2026-10-03 03:00" --no-pager

# follow one request across services by its ID
grep -r "req_id=8f3a2c" /var/log/app/ | sort

# what changed on disk recently?
find /etc -mmin -60 -type f

This is why structured logging matters. Plain strings are for humans; JSON lines with consistent fields are for humans with jq. Log a request ID, user ID, version and duration on every line, and correlation stops being guesswork:

jq -c 'select(.level == "error" and .version == "2.14.0")' app.log \
  | jq -r '.msg' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

Let git bisect find the commit

If it worked last week and it's broken now, the answer is somewhere in the history. git bisect does a binary search over commits: a thousand commits take about ten steps.

git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.13.0

# automate it with your reproduction script (exit 0 = good)
git bisect run ./scripts/repro.sh

git bisect reset

Automated bisect plus a reliable reproduction is the closest thing to magic in this job.

When the code looks fine: strace

Sometimes the application swears it's doing the right thing. strace shows what it actually asks the kernel to do: which files it opens, which sockets it connects to, which calls fail and why.

# attach to a running process, follow forks, show file and network calls
sudo strace -f -p 4242 -e trace=file,network -s 200

# summary of syscalls and errors
strace -c -f ./worker --once

An ENOENT on a config path, an EACCES on a socket, a connect() that hangs for 30 seconds on a DNS server that no longer exists. These are invisible from inside the app and obvious from outside. Use it on a staging host first; tracing adds overhead.

Root cause vs symptom

When the error disappears, you're not done. Ask why five times. The disk filled up. Why? Logs weren't rotated. Why? The logrotate config was in the old image. Why? The new image was built from a different base. Why? Nobody owns the base image. That last answer is the root cause, and it's the one that keeps you from being paged again next month.

Fix the symptom to stop the bleeding. Fix the cause so it doesn't come back. Then write down what you learned, because future you will not remember.

Every Linux box runs things you didn't start. Daemons: background processes that come up at boot, listen on ports, and wait. Most are harmless. Some are leftovers from a package you installed once and forgot. A few are listening on every interface for no reason at all. Each one is code with privileges and a potential door. If you don't know what's running on your machine, someone else might find out first.

What is running

On any systemd distribution, start with the service manager. It knows what it launched and why.

# services running right now
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

# services enabled to start at boot
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled

# timers are daemons too, just scheduled ones
systemctl list-timers --all

For each name you don't recognize, ask systemd what it is and where it came from:

systemctl status cups.service
systemctl cat cups.service          # the unit file, including overrides
dpkg -S /usr/sbin/cupsd             # which package owns it (rpm -qf on Fedora/RHEL)

Who is listening

A daemon that only talks to localhost is a much smaller risk than one bound to 0.0.0.0. ss replaced netstat years ago and tells you exactly what's listening and which process owns it.

sudo ss -tulpn

Read the Local Address:Port column carefully:

  • 127.0.0.1:5432 or [::1]:5432 — reachable only from this machine.
  • 0.0.0.0:5432 or *:5432 or [::]:5432 — reachable from any network the host is on.
  • 192.168.1.10:8080 — bound to one specific interface.

A database listening on all interfaces on a laptop that joins café Wi-Fi is a classic. So is a dev server someone started with --host 0.0.0.0 and never stopped. Then double-check from the outside, from another machine you own, with nmap against your own host only.

Processes systemd didn't start

Not everything is a unit. Look at the process tree for things that run outside the service manager: user crontabs, shells left in tmux, containers, or something worse.

ps -eo pid,user,etime,cmd --forest | less

# per-user cron jobs and system-wide ones
sudo ls /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ /etc/cron.d/

# open network connections per process
sudo lsof -i -P -n | grep -v LISTEN

A process with a strange name running from /tmp or /dev/shm, owned by your web server user, deserves your full attention. Isolate the host before you poke at it.

Disable what you don't need

The most secure service is the one that isn't running. On a server, ask of every daemon: does this machine's job require it? If not:

# stop it now and keep it from starting at boot
sudo systemctl disable --now avahi-daemon.service

# make sure nothing else can start it, either
sudo systemctl mask avahi-daemon.service avahi-daemon.socket

# or just remove the package
sudo apt purge avahi-daemon

Note the socket unit. Socket activation means a service can be started on demand by a connection, so disabling only the .service isn't always enough.

For daemons you do need, bind them to localhost or a private interface, put a host firewall in front (ufw or nftables, default deny inbound), and look at systemd's sandboxing options: systemd-analyze security nginx.service scores a unit and lists hardening directives like ProtectSystem=, NoNewPrivileges= and PrivateTmp=.

Make it a routine

Save the output of ss -tulpn and systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled to a file. Diff it next month. Anything new should have a reason you can explain. If you can't explain it, that's your answer.

Every week a few hundred new vulnerabilities get published. You can't patch them all at once, and you shouldn't try to read them all. What you need is a system: know what you run, know which flaws matter, and fix the dangerous ones before someone uses them. Attackers don't need a zero-day when a two-year-old bug is still sitting unpatched on your edge. This post is about how vulnerabilities are tracked, and how to triage them without drowning.

CVE: a name for every flaw

A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID is a unique identifier like CVE-2021-44228, the Log4Shell bug. It doesn't tell you how bad something is. It just makes sure everyone is talking about the same flaw. CVE IDs are assigned by CNAs (CVE Numbering Authorities), usually the vendor or project itself, and the records are enriched in databases such as the NVD and in vendor and distribution security trackers.

Your distribution's tracker is often the most useful view, because it tells you which package version in your release fixes the issue. Backported fixes mean the version number may look old and still be patched.

CVSS, KEV and EPSS: three different questions

SignalAnswersUse it for
CVSSHow severe is this in theory?A 0–10 score from base metrics like attack vector, complexity and impact.
CISA KEVIs it being exploited in the wild right now?The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. If it's listed and you run it, it's urgent.
EPSSHow likely is exploitation soon?A probability estimate from FIRST, useful for ranking a long backlog.

CVSS alone is a bad prioritization tool: a huge share of CVEs score "high" or "critical", and most of them will never be exploited. Combine signals. A 7.5 on an internet-facing service listed in KEV beats a 9.8 in a library function you never call.

Know what you run: SBOMs and scanning

You can't patch what you don't know you have. A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is an inventory of every component in a build, direct and transitive, in a standard format like CycloneDX or SPDX. Generate one per release and keep it, so that next time a big CVE drops you can answer "are we affected?" in minutes instead of days.

# generate an SBOM for a container image or a directory
syft my-app:2.14.0 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

# scan the SBOM (or the image directly) for known vulnerabilities
grype sbom:./sbom.json --only-fixed

# language-native audits
npm audit --omit=dev
pip-audit
bundle audit check --update

Run these in CI. Enable Dependabot or Renovate so updates arrive as small, reviewable pull requests instead of one terrifying quarterly upgrade.

A patch discipline that actually works

  1. Inventory. SBOMs for your apps, an asset list for your hosts. Unknown assets are where breaches live.
  2. Triage by exposure. Internet-facing and in KEV first. Then high EPSS. Then everything else on a schedule.
  3. Set target windows. For example: actively exploited and exposed within 48 hours, critical within 7 days, the rest in the next regular cycle. Write them down and measure them.
  4. Mitigate when you can't patch. Disable the feature, restrict network access, add a WAF rule, rotate credentials. Mitigation buys time; it isn't a fix.
  5. Verify. Rescan after patching. "We deployed it" and "it's fixed everywhere" are different statements.
⚠️
"Not reachable" is a hypothesis, not a fact. Prove it, or patch anyway.

The point

Vulnerability management isn't glamorous. It's spreadsheets, scanners and small pull requests. But nearly every major breach story has the same line somewhere in the middle: a patch was available. Don't be that line.

The easiest system to break into isn't a server. It's a person. People are helpful, busy, polite and afraid of getting in trouble, and every one of those traits can be turned against them. Firewalls don't stop a phone call from "IT support". Encryption doesn't stop someone from reading a one-time code aloud to a stranger. If you want to defend a team, you have to understand why social engineering works, and then build a culture where people feel safe saying "wait, this seems off".

Why it works

Social engineering doesn't exploit stupidity. It exploits normal human shortcuts that usually serve us well.

  • Authority. A message that seems to come from the CEO, a bank, or the police gets obeyed with less scrutiny.
  • Urgency. "Your account will be closed in one hour." Time pressure shuts down careful thinking. That's the whole point.
  • Pretexting. A plausible backstory: a new hire who can't log in, a vendor with an updated invoice, a courier at the door. The story makes the request feel routine.
  • Reciprocity and liking. Someone who was friendly or did you a small favor is easier to say yes to.
  • Social proof. "Everyone on your team has already completed this form."
  • Fear. Of looking incompetent, of slowing down the boss, of breaking the rules by asking questions.

These attacks rarely look sophisticated. They look like a normal Tuesday.

Red flags

No checklist catches everything, but most attempts share some of these traits:

  1. An unexpected request to move money, change bank details, or buy gift cards.
  2. A request for credentials, MFA codes, or approval of a login push you didn't start. No legitimate team needs your one-time code.
  3. Pressure to skip normal process: "no time for the ticket", "keep this confidential".
  4. A channel switch: an email that asks you to continue on WhatsApp or a personal number.
  5. Lookalike domains, display names that don't match the address, links whose real destination differs from the text.
  6. Voice or video that feels slightly wrong. Cloned voices and deepfakes are cheap now; a familiar voice is no longer proof of identity.

Verify out of band

The single most effective defense is simple: when a request is sensitive, verify it through a channel you already trust, not one provided in the message. Hang up and call the number in the company directory. Message the person on the internal chat. Walk to their desk.

Back it with process so nobody has to be a hero. Payment detail changes require a callback to a known number. Password resets require identity checks the help desk can't skip. Admin actions require a second approver. And prefer phishing-resistant MFA, like passkeys and security keys, so that even a convincing fake page gets nothing useful.

Build a reporting culture

People will be fooled. Good people, senior people, security people. What determines the damage is how fast someone reports it. That speed depends entirely on whether reporting is safe.

  • Make it one click. A "report phishing" button, a dedicated chat channel, a short alias like security@.
  • Thank every report, including false alarms. Especially false alarms.
  • Never punish the click. Shame teaches people to hide mistakes, and hidden mistakes become incidents.
  • Share real examples (sanitized) of attempts that targeted your team. Stories stick better than slide decks.
  • Measure reporting rate, not only click rate. A team that reports quickly is a team that's hard to compromise.

The attacker's best tool is your team's reluctance to ask a simple question. Take that tool away. Make "let me verify that" the most normal sentence in the office.

Time is the dependency nobody lists. TLS checks it. Kerberos checks it. Your one-time codes are computed from it. Your logs are only as useful as the timestamps on them. When a clock drifts, things fail in ways that look like anything except a clock problem: "invalid certificate", "token expired", "signature not yet valid", an incident timeline that makes no sense. Time is an attack surface, and it's also a reliability problem hiding in plain sight.

What breaks when clocks are wrong

  • TLS. Certificates have notBefore and notAfter dates. A client whose clock is in the past rejects valid certificates; a clock far in the future accepts nothing.
  • TOTP. Authenticator codes are derived from the current 30-second window. Most servers tolerate one step of drift; beyond that, codes silently fail.
  • Kerberos and Active Directory. Default maximum skew is five minutes. Beyond that, authentication stops.
  • Signed tokens. JWT exp, nbf and iat claims, presigned cloud URLs, webhook signatures with timestamps. All of them assume your clock agrees with the issuer's.
  • Distributed systems. Ordering events by wall-clock time across hosts is fragile even with good NTP. Use logical clocks or sequence numbers where order truly matters.

Keep clocks honest with NTP

Every machine should sync time continuously, not once at boot. On most modern Linux systems that's systemd-timesyncd or chrony.

# is the clock synchronized?
timedatectl status

# chrony: current offset and the sources in use
chronyc tracking
chronyc sources -v

Look for System clock synchronized: yes and an offset in milliseconds, not seconds. Use several sources so one bad server can be outvoted, and in VMs and containers make sure someone, the host or the guest, is actually keeping time. NTP traffic isn't authenticated by default; where it matters, chrony supports NTS (Network Time Security), which adds authentication on top of NTP.

Log in UTC. Always.

Timezones are a presentation concern. Store and log in UTC, in ISO 8601 with an explicit offset, and convert only when you show a time to a human.

# set servers to UTC
sudo timedatectl set-timezone UTC

# ISO 8601 timestamps from the shell
date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"

Why it matters: daylight saving time creates an hour that happens twice and an hour that never happens. If your logs are in local time, an incident that crosses a DST change, or spans servers in two regions, becomes a puzzle. During an investigation you will be correlating firewall logs, application logs and cloud audit trails. They need one timeline.

Certificate expiry is a scheduled outage

Expired certificates are the most predictable outage in the industry, and it still happens to everyone. Automate renewal (ACME with Let's Encrypt or your CA), and monitor expiry independently of the renewal job, because the renewal job is the thing that will break.

# days until a certificate expires
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -enddate

# fail if it expires within 14 days (exit code 1)
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -checkend $((14*86400))

Certificate lifetimes are getting shorter across the industry, which makes manual renewal untenable. Treat that as a feature: short-lived certificates force you to automate, and automation doesn't forget.

A short checklist

  1. NTP or chrony running and synchronized on every host.
  2. Servers in UTC; logs in ISO 8601 with offsets.
  3. Alerts on clock offset above a threshold.
  4. Automated certificate renewal, plus independent expiry monitoring.
  5. Token validation with a small, explicit clock-skew allowance.

Time won't announce itself as the problem. You have to check.

Nobody cares about backups. Everybody cares about restores. The difference is usually discovered at 2 a.m., after a disk dies, a script runs rm -rf on the wrong path, or ransomware encrypts everything it can reach, including the backup drive that was conveniently plugged in. A mirror of your data is only useful if it's separate from the original in every way that matters. Here's how to build backups you can trust.

The 3-2-1 rule

  • 3 copies of your data: the original plus two backups.
  • 2 different media or systems, so one failure mode can't take out both.
  • 1 copy off-site, so a fire, flood or theft doesn't either.

A modern extension is 3-2-1-1-0: add one copy that's offline or immutable, and aim for zero errors in verified restores. That last part is the one people skip.

RAID is not a backup

RAID protects against a disk failing. That's it. It faithfully mirrors your mistakes in real time: delete a file and it's deleted on every disk; ransomware encrypts both halves of the mirror at once; filesystem corruption is replicated perfectly. Same goes for sync tools like Dropbox or a live rsync mirror: sync is availability, backup is history. You need versions, going back in time, that can't be changed by whatever just went wrong.

Tools: rsync and restic

rsync is perfect for mirroring and moving data efficiently. With --link-dest it can even build cheap daily snapshots using hard links:

TODAY=$(date -u +%F)
rsync -aH --delete \
  --link-dest=/backup/latest \
  /home/ /backup/$TODAY/ \
&& ln -sfn /backup/$TODAY /backup/latest

For real backups I prefer restic: encrypted, deduplicated, snapshot-based, and it speaks to local disks, SFTP and S3-compatible storage.

export RESTIC_REPOSITORY=s3:s3.example.com/my-backups
export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE=~/.config/restic/pass

restic init                                   # once
restic backup ~/projects ~/documents --exclude-caches
restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12 --prune
restic check --read-data-subset=5%            # verify repository integrity

Keep the repository password somewhere that survives losing the machine. An encrypted backup with a lost key is just expensive noise.

Test your restores

A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. Schedule restore drills:

restic snapshots
restic restore latest --target /tmp/restore-test --include ~/projects/api
diff -r ~/projects/api /tmp/restore-test/home/elliot/projects/api && echo "restore OK"

For databases, restore the dump into a fresh instance and run a query that proves the data is there. Time it. Your recovery time objective is whatever the drill actually took, not what the wiki says.

Ransomware-resistant copies

Modern ransomware goes looking for backups first. Design so that a compromised machine can't destroy its own history:

  1. Pull, don't push. A backup server that pulls from clients can't be wiped by credentials stolen from a client.
  2. Append-only access. restic's REST server supports --append-only; clients can add snapshots but not delete them.
  3. Immutable storage. S3 Object Lock (compliance mode) or a provider's equivalent keeps objects undeletable for a retention period.
  4. Offline media. A drive that's unplugged and in a drawer can't be encrypted remotely. Rotate it.
  5. Separate credentials. Backup admin accounts shouldn't share identity, SSO or passwords with production.

Every system fails eventually. The question is whether it's a bad afternoon or the end of the company.

It always arrives the same way. A link in a group chat, a vendor advisory with no patch yet, a headline with a catchy name. A zero-day is a vulnerability that's being exploited before a fix is available, or before you've had time to apply it. You can't prevent it from existing. What you control is the next 72 hours: how fast you know whether you're exposed, how well you contain it, and how calmly you communicate. Panic is not a plan. This is.

Hour 0: triage

Open an incident channel, name an incident commander, and start a timestamped log. Then answer three questions, in order:

  1. Do we run it? Search your SBOMs, asset inventory, container images and cloud resources. This is where all that boring inventory work pays off.
  2. Is it exposed? Internet-facing, reachable from untrusted networks, or only internal? Which version, which configuration?
  3. Is there evidence it was used against us? Check logs for the indicators published in the advisory, going back to before the disclosure date. Exploitation usually starts before the news.
# which releases ship the affected component? (CycloneDX SBOMs)
for f in sboms/*.json; do
  jq -r --arg f "$f" '.components[]? | select(.name == "affected-package") | "\($f)  \(.version)"' "$f"
done

# which hosts have it installed?
ansible all -m shell -a "dpkg -l affected-package 2>/dev/null | tail -n1"

Contain before you cure

If there's no patch yet, reduce exposure. Containment is about buying time without destroying evidence.

  • Apply the vendor's mitigation: a config flag, a disabled module, an environment variable.
  • Restrict network access: pull the service off the internet, allowlist source IPs, add a WAF rule for the known request pattern.
  • Isolate suspected compromised hosts from the network, but don't wipe them yet. Snapshot disks and capture memory if you can.
  • Rotate credentials and tokens the affected system could access. Assume anything it could read is now known.

Communicate on a schedule

Silence breeds rumors. Post updates at a fixed cadence, every hour early on, even if the update is "no change". Keep separate audiences in mind:

AudienceWhat they need
RespondersCurrent status, owners, next actions, what not to touch.
LeadershipExposure, business impact, decisions needed, next update time.
CustomersWhat's affected, what you're doing, what they should do. Facts only.
Legal and complianceWhether personal data may be involved; notification deadlines may apply.

Never speculate in external communications. "We are investigating" is honest. "No data was accessed" before you've checked is a liability.

Patch, verify, watch

When the fix ships, roll it out by exposure: internet-facing first. Verify each system actually runs the fixed version, then rescan. Keep heightened monitoring for weeks. Early patches are sometimes incomplete, and a follow-up CVE for the same component is common. If you found evidence of compromise, patching closes the door; it doesn't remove whoever already walked in. Rebuild affected systems from known-good images.

⚠️
Patching a compromised host is not remediation. Rebuild it, rotate its secrets, and keep the evidence.

The blameless postmortem

Within a week, while memories are fresh, write it down. Blameless doesn't mean nobody is accountable; it means you assume people made reasonable decisions with the information they had, and you fix the system that gave them bad information.

  • A timeline: detection, decisions, actions, with timestamps in UTC.
  • What went well. Repeat it on purpose next time.
  • Where you were slow: finding assets, getting approvals, reaching people.
  • Action items with owners and dates, not "be more careful".

Control is an illusion. Preparation isn't. The teams that handle zero-days well aren't faster typists; they just did the inventory before they needed it.

Silence breeds rumors. Post updates at a fixed cadence, every hour early on, even if the update is "no change". Keep separate audiences in mind:

When the fix ships, roll it out by exposure: internet-facing first. Verify each system actually runs the fixed version, then rescan. Keep heightened monitoring for weeks. Within a week, while memories are fresh, write it down. Blameless doesn't mean nobody is accountable; it means you assume people made reasonable decisions with the information they had, and you fix the system that gave them bad information.

 * Action items with owners and dates, not "be more careful".

posts.html:
You can hide your name and still be found. The photo you posted has GPS coordinates in it. The PDF you shared lists your full name, your employer's username format and the exact software you wrote it with. Your browser hands out enough small details to be recognized across sites without a single cookie. Metadata is data about data, and it's usually more revealing than the content itself. The good news: most of it is easy to see, and easy to remove.

EXIF: your photos talk

Cameras and phones embed EXIF metadata in images: device make and model, lens, timestamps, sometimes the owner's name or serial number, and, if location is enabled, GPS coordinates precise to a few meters. Many big platforms strip EXIF on upload. Plenty of others don't: personal blogs, forums, direct file shares, email attachments, cloud folders.

# see everything embedded in a photo
exiftool IMG_2041.jpg

# just the interesting bits
exiftool -gps:all -model -datetimeoriginal -serialnumber IMG_2041.jpg

Documents remember who wrote them

Office files and PDFs carry author names, company, last-modified-by, creation tool and version, revision history, and sometimes tracked changes and comments you thought you'd deleted. In a corporate setting, author fields leak usernames, which reveal the naming convention for accounts. That's useful reconnaissance for anyone planning a phishing campaign, which is exactly why you should clean what you publish.

exiftool -a -G1 report.pdf | grep -Ei "author|creator|producer|company"
exiftool report.docx

Also check for content-level leaks that no metadata tool will catch: hidden sheets, hidden rows, speaker notes, and "redactions" made by drawing a black box over text that's still selectable underneath.

How to strip it

exiftool can remove metadata in place. mat2 (Metadata Anonymisation Toolkit) goes further, understanding many formats and cleaning them more thoroughly.

# remove all writable metadata from images (keeps an _original backup)
exiftool -all= *.jpg

# overwrite without backups, recursively
exiftool -all= -overwrite_original -r ./to-publish/

# mat2: inspect, then clean (writes file.cleaned.ext)
mat2 --show report.pdf
mat2 report.pdf photo.jpg slides.odp

Verify after cleaning by running exiftool again. For PDFs, re-exporting from a clean source is often more reliable than scrubbing. For phones, turn off location tagging in the camera app unless you actually want it.

Browser fingerprinting

Even without cookies, a website can combine dozens of small signals into a fairly stable identifier: user agent, screen size, timezone, language, installed fonts, GPU details exposed by canvas and WebGL rendering, audio processing quirks, and more. No single value identifies you; the combination often does.

  • Blend in rather than stand out. Ten privacy extensions can make you more unique, not less.
  • Use a browser with built-in protections. Tor Browser makes every user look alike; Firefox's resist-fingerprinting mode and Brave's randomization reduce the signal.
  • Separate identities. Different browser profiles or containers for work, personal and anything sensitive.
  • Test yourself with the EFF's Cover Your Tracks to see how unique your browser looks.

Habits worth keeping

  1. Strip metadata before anything leaves your machine for a public place.
  2. Add a metadata-cleaning step to the publishing pipeline of your site or docs.
  3. Review documents for hidden content, not just metadata.
  4. Assume anything you publish will be downloaded and inspected, byte by byte.

Privacy isn't one big secret. It's a thousand small details you chose not to leave behind.

The screen freezes. A wall of hex scrolls past, ending in Kernel panic - not syncing. The instinct is to reboot and hope. Resist it, at least for a minute. A kernel panic or oops is the kernel's own crash report, and it usually tells you exactly where things went wrong, if you capture it before it's gone. This is a practical guide to reading one, and to collecting what you'll need to find the cause.

Oops vs panic

An oops is the kernel detecting a serious error, like a bad pointer dereference in a driver, logging it, and killing the offending task. The system often keeps running, but in an unknown state. Treat it as tainted. A panic is fatal: the kernel decides it can't continue safely and halts (or reboots, if kernel.panic is set). Many panics start life as an oops that hit something critical, or a system configured with panic_on_oops=1.

Reading the report

A typical oops has the same anatomy. Read it top to bottom:

BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000008
#PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode
Oops: 0000 [#1] PREEMPT SMP NOPTI
CPU: 3 PID: 1187 Comm: kworker/3:2 Tainted: P           O      6.8.0-45-generic
Hardware name: ...
RIP: 0010:foo_driver_poll+0x2a/0x90 [foo_driver]
Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 process_one_work+0x16f/0x350
 worker_thread+0x2f5/0x410
 kthread+0xe8/0x120
 </TASK>
  • The first line is the reason: a NULL dereference, a general protection fault, a soft lockup, out of memory.
  • Comm and PID tell you which task was running.
  • Tainted flags matter: P means a proprietary module was loaded, O an out-of-tree module, E an unsigned one. Upstream developers will ask you to reproduce without them.
  • RIP is the instruction that faulted. function+offset/length [module] points straight at the culprit, here an out-of-tree driver.
  • Call Trace is how execution got there, most recent first.

What to collect before rebooting

If the machine is still alive after an oops, grab everything now. After a reboot, the ring buffer is gone.

# the kernel ring buffer, with readable timestamps
sudo dmesg -T > ~/oops-$(date -u +%FT%H%M).txt

# kernel messages from the previous boot (needs persistent journal)
journalctl -k -b -1 --no-pager

# context: exact kernel, loaded modules, taint value
uname -a
lsmod > ~/lsmod.txt
cat /proc/sys/kernel/tainted

Make sure the journal persists across reboots, or -b -1 will be empty: create /var/log/journal or set Storage=persistent in journald.conf. Also note what changed recently: a kernel update, a new driver, a firmware upgrade, new hardware.

kdump: catch the full crash

For a full panic, nothing survives in RAM unless you planned for it. kdump reserves memory for a small crash kernel; when the main kernel panics, the crash kernel boots and writes a vmcore to disk for later analysis with the crash utility.

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install kdump-tools
# Fedora/RHEL
sudo dnf install kexec-tools && sudo systemctl enable --now kdump

# after a reboot, verify it's armed
kdump-config show      # Debian/Ubuntu
kdumpctl status        # Fedora/RHEL

Dumps land in /var/crash/. On production servers, enable kdump before you need it. It's the difference between "it crashed" and "here is the exact state of memory when it crashed".

Common causes

  1. Drivers, especially out-of-tree and proprietary ones (GPU, Wi-Fi, storage controllers).
  2. Bad RAM. Random panics in unrelated places point to hardware. Run memtest86+ overnight.
  3. Kernel regressions after an update. Boot the previous kernel from the bootloader menu to confirm.
  4. Filesystem or storage errors, often preceded by I/O errors in the log.
  5. Overheating and power issues, which look random until you check the sensors.

A panic feels like the end of the world. It's just the kernel being honest about something it couldn't handle. Listen to it.

This post collects the visual elements of the fsociety theme and the options you can change in the Ghost admin. Use it as a reference when writing: everything here comes out of Ghost's standard editor, with no special HTML.

Palette

The theme is built for the dark: near-black surfaces, warm off-white text, and one red that shows up only where it matters (cursor, links, buttons, focus and the occasional glitch). The blue comes from the Kali terminal prompt.

The red comes from Ghost's Accent color (Design & branding → Brand). Recommended: #E0182D.

Typography

Headings and body text are set in Archivo. Post titles, metadata, the terminal prompt and code are set in JetBrains Mono, so every title reads like a filename. If you pick another font in Design & branding → Typography, it replaces Archivo.

A paragraph with bold, italic, a link and inline code. Body text sits slightly off pure white, which keeps long reads comfortable on a black background.

Heading level 2

Use H2 for the main sections of a post.

Heading level 3

Use H3 for subsections.

Heading level 4

Use H4 for smaller groups.

Title your posts like episodes

fsociety works best when every post title is an episode filename: epsS.E_name.ext. Season and episode, an underscore, a name in leetspeak if you like, and an extension. The extension tells you the season:

  • Season 1 — video containers: .mov .mpeg .mkv .mp4 .wmv .asf .flv .m4v .qt .avi.
  • Season 2 — encryption formats, like .tc, .ksd and .asec.
  • Season 3 — code and archive files.
  • Season 4 — HTTP 4xx status codes. The theme's 404 page mirrors this season.

Hello, friend. I'm Elliot. By day I'm a cybersecurity engineer: I watch logs, chase alerts, patch things before they break, and explain to people why the thing they want to do is a bad idea. By night I write here, about security, Linux and the quiet systems that run the world while nobody's looking.

whoami

The short version, in the only format I trust:

$ whoami
elliot

$ id
uid=1000(elliot) gid=1000(elliot) groups=1000(elliot),27(sudo),4(adm)

$ sudo -l
[sudo] password for elliot:
Sorry, user elliot may not run sudo on fsociety. This incident will be reported.

I'm in the adm group, so I can read the logs. That's most of the job, honestly.

What I write about

Every post here is titled like an episode file, but the content is real. No hype, no fear-selling, no exploit dumps. Just the things I wish someone had explained to me earlier:

  • Defensive security: threat models, vulnerability triage, incident response, social engineering awareness.
  • Linux internals: daemons, kernels, clocks, the stuff under the desktop.
  • Engineering habits: debugging, backups, logging, reading raw bytes when the tools lie.
  • Privacy: metadata, fingerprinting, and how much you leave behind without noticing.

If something here is wrong, tell me. I'd rather be corrected than confidently wrong in public.

Contact

Subscribe to get new posts by email. If you want to talk, the links in the footer work. I read everything. I don't always answer. Don't take it personally; I don't answer most people.

About this site
